comments.name: Austin Ouellette
comments.body:
I’m a corporate accountant.

ASC 275, which is the US law codifying risk assessment and reserves for risk, is probably the most important law concerning this IPO.

ASC 275 is the law that requires publicly traded companies to disclose known or estimated material risks. What does that mean? It means, if you’re a mortgage broker like the now defunct Countrywide Financial, you’re supposed to disclose the risks you know about. Risks like knowingly selling mortgages to people who can’t afford them and are likely to default.

You’re also, by law, supposed to set aside a reserve to cover losses stemming from such risks. If you’re an oil company, for example, you’re required to set aside a reserve to deal with spill cleanup and legal challenges, and you’re supposed to disclose those risks in your financial statements.

How do you even do that with an AI company? *Our product might decide to take it upon itself to exterminate the human race, or, it might take it upon itself to infiltrate government systems to manipulate markets or perform social engineering for its own ends beyond our control.* How do you possibly begin to address that risk?

In my professional opinion? It’s impossible to operate a fiscally responsible AI company. I think it’s mathematically impossible to create a sufficient enough reserve to protect the company from reasonable risks associated with its products.

That’s not including the moral question of creating a product that might kill us all.

Well, Xi's purge mania makes it clear that it is a very good thing indeed that the U.S. has a two-term limit on its presidents. While it is true that the 22nd Amendment was ratified in part out of spite by New Deal-hating Republicans who never wanted to see another Democrat like FDR get elected 4 times, the most notable impact of the amendment since ratification in 1951 is that not one U.S. president has died non-violently in office since FDR himself passed away in April 1945.

There is absolutely no good argument for having a top elected political leader or anybody else with power serve until a non-violent death or incapacitation. Name me one if you can. Has anything good arisen from seeing 3 Supreme Court justices (Rehnquist in 2005, Scalia in 2016, Ginsburg in 2020) die on the bench in this century?

No Chinese leader has been in power until death since Mao Zedong passed away 50 years ago in 1976. Objectively speaking, the half-century since has been one of the greatest and most glorious periods in the 5,000 year history of Chinese civilization. The country has changed in that time from a failed state economic basket case into a superpower. Having a clear succession procedure via what was an informal 2-term limit on the top leader undoubtedly helped.

Not sure if China will keep it up if Xi clings to power as an octogenarian or even nonagenarian autocrat a la Mao or somebody today like Paul Biya (now 93 years old) in Cameroon.

Term limits. They are good and worth keeping.

We tend to theorize about our species as if we are separate from  the natural behavioral evolution of other organisms on this planet, animal or plant.  We are not.  To be "absorbed, through mating" is hybridization.  To be all the same species, Homo sapiens, is to be monotypic.  Diverse expressions of a single species is to be a subspecies, breed (animals) or a cultivar or variety (plants) which supports adaption to a diversity of ecosystems and niches.  

A monoculture (monocrop), all one species and all one cultivar, is extremely vulnerable to the other biological kingdoms that include bacteria, viruses and fungi (pandemics).  The more we become the same genetically, and the more we homogenize our living environments and the foods we eat, the more chance of a mass die-off there is.  That is the natural trajectory of most species that have rapid population growth behaviors (aggression, invasiveness, weediness) - dominant population booms and crashes.  Perhaps, Homo sapiens was the more successful breeding population?  In the long run, that comes, inherently, with its own vulnerabilities.  Natural law will always seek to find balance.

comments.name: wolczr
comments.body:
Now let’s do some horizon scanning.

Biological evolution took about 6 million years to take our ancestors from chimp-level cognition to modern human brains. AI went from GPT-2, which could barely stay coherent in 2019, to expert-level performance on many reasoning, coding, and knowledge tasks in about 7 years. Treat those as comparable leaps and AI is improving roughly 100,000 to 1,000,000 times faster than biological evolution.

The fairer comparison is cultural evolution, since humans have gotten dramatically smarter collectively through language, writing, math, science, and computing, all on the same biological hardware. Going from hunter-gatherer knowledge to a modern knowledge economy took roughly 10,000 to 50,000 years. Against that, AI is moving about 1,000 to 10,000 times faster.

There's a wrinkle: if you measure individual intelligence instead, like the Flynn effect's gain of about 3 IQ points per decade, the gap shrinks to something like 10x, though comparing IQ tests to AI benchmarks is shaky at best.

Big caveats apply. These are loose analogies, not precise measurements. AI is narrower than humans in some ways and broader in others. And AI isn't an independent competitor, since it's trained on the accumulated output of human culture, so it's partly a product of that very process. Still, even with generous error bars, the pace is hard to comprehend, and it may be accelerating.

Since we fininished our renovations, we began taking on droves of American family here every summer. When we close out the season, we find all sorts of food remnants in the bedding, on the floor, under sofa cushions and even in the bathroom. Yes. The bathroom. This is a huge problem because we literally JUST got ahead of our pest problem. 

So last summer, we implemented a "no-food-outside-of-kitchen/dining-area-policy". The reaction was hostile. You would have thought I had proposed the mass murder of kittens in a Midsommar-style ritual. So I think this whole snacking thing is actually an addiction, because even the mildest pushback results in an animalistic over-reaction. It is sad really, because when my partner's family visit from Cuba, they think the policy is a total given.

The first paragraphs primarily identify the cultural references of small magazines or websites the critic feels we might have missed, or that we might not be able to find Block island on a map. When we finally get around to the novel itself, the unintended laughter begins. First, "Wetish College" in Wisconsin must be the most lugubrious name for a fictional institution of higher learning since H. P. Lovecraft investigated occult goings-on at Miskatonic University. Second, would-be witches read Edith Wharton and not Flannery O'Connor? And Sherwood Anderson, author of the dark and compulsive novel "Winesburg, Ohio" a "grounded"-and "down-to-earth" writer? I also find no comparison to the novel The Secret History., which is told from the view of a non-privileged outsider. That's a narrative wisdom that Chad Harbach lacked when he first began writing this novel.

“Owen had only ever wanted to be a fop” is the promising first sentence of the novel (and “foppery was very much a growth industry,” the second paragraph adds), but I rather think the reviewer gets it wrong about the protagonist. The reviewer describes him as shallow and compares him to Flashman. Not quite. “Unserious,” perhaps. But he’s more in line with a fairly common Stephenson protagonist, an obvious stand-in for both reader and author, who is smart and decent enough but finds himself in bemusing, perilous, often world-historical situations and mostly rises to the occasion. I’m only a third of the way through and may be proved wrong. But so far Owen, the would-be fop, seems not so much shallow as a man with a gift for walking into situations in which everyone else knows a great deal more about what’s going on than he, and doing so with a fair amount of aplomb. 

I might add, in response to another comment, that if you can get through the first hundred pages of Cryptonomicon—I couldn’t, the first time around, although I love those pages now—the rest of the book will serve as an incalculable reward. I feel the same way about Anathem, which offers many satisfactions and surprises.

Mr. Halzen points out why it is so hard for us humans to understand of the inner working of nature. From birth to death we experience the world around us with the gauges our body has, Eyes, Ears, Touch, Smell. These gauges are very limited - a tiny bit of spectrum of electromagnetic waves. 20Hz to 20,000 Hz in sound waves, certainly no neutrinos. Atoms, Electrons, Neutrinos, photons are abstract entities which existence we derive mathematically from observed entities. And even these derived entities are quantum mysteries: Waves or particles popping up only with probability amplitudes. The human brain is a marvelous device.

I hope most readers do not miss the message he brings for discussion, which is that basic science is very well worth doing despite those who try to control the purse strings demanding results that are useful within a year or certainly a decade.  This applies to all branches of science and while a popular idea a couple generations ago, has lost favor with the mentality of silicon valley.

Careful research by well trained scientists is the bedrock of all the disciplines, and we are seeing that shoved aside by corporations willing to force their researchers to hide negative results in order to bring products to market.  

Universities should be well funded to allow long term projects to find out what makes nature work.

Dr. Halzen's work and position at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, is to be celebrated and a proud addition to the Laurates Madison has fostered.
